title: Mini case - reading the yield curve
subtitle: A practical application: reading the yield curve to guess the economic cycle
openingQuestion: You see a 2-year bond yielding 4.8% and a 10-year bond yielding 4.2%. What does this signal tell you?
openingOptions: Yield must always rise with maturity, so this data is wrong
This is an inverted yield curve (2-year > 10-year) - the market is pricing in a recession or the Fed cutting rates within 1-2 years
It means nothing, just market noise
The economy is booming, so invest heavily in cyclical stocks
explanation: Reading a yield curve means reading market expectations, not any single institution's forecast. When the two-year yield exceeds the ten-year yield, the market is saying that the current level of rates is too high for the economy to bear and will have to come down. The thing to be careful about with this signal is the lag: the gap between an inversion and an actual recession has ranged from a few months to over two years.

realWorldExample.description: The US yield curve inverted the deepest in over 40 years during 2022-2023 as the Fed hiked rates aggressively to fight inflation - many economists forecast a recession based on this signal.

quiz.question: If you're a bond investor and believe interest rates are about to drop sharply, what strategy makes sense?
options: Buy floating-rate bonds to track the market
Buy short-maturity bonds to limit price swings
Move the entire portfolio to cash and wait
Buy long-maturity bonds to capture the largest price gain
quiz.explanation: Long-maturity bonds have higher duration → more sensitive to changes in rates. If the rate-cut call is right, long-maturity bond prices rise more sharply, producing a larger capital gain than short-maturity bonds.

quiz.question: If you see a yield curve that is almost completely FLAT (yields at every maturity nearly equal) instead of clearly upward-sloping or inverted, what stage of the economic cycle does this usually reflect?
options: A transition stage, where the market hasn't settled on a direction yet
The middle of a strong and stable growth cycle
The stage right after the central bank makes deep rate cuts
A stage of high inflation persisting continuously for years
quiz.explanation: A flat yield curve usually shows up in the transition between a tightening and an easing cycle - the market is "balancing" between different scenarios, making it a more ambiguous signal (needing to be combined with other data) than a clearly sloped or deeply inverted curve.

quiz.question: The 2-year yield is 4.8%, the 10-year yield is 4.1%. What state is the curve in?
options: Normal upward slope, since both are above 4%
Inverted, because the short maturity pays more than the long maturity
Flat, because the gap is under one percentage point
Cannot be concluded without a 30-year yield
quiz.explanation: 10-year minus 2-year equals negative 0.7 points, a clear inversion. The market is betting rates will have to fall sharply - something that usually only happens when the economy is turning down.

quiz.question: Why isn't an inverted curve a signal to sell all your stocks right away?
options: Because an inversion is actually a sign of strong economic growth
Because the signal only holds for the US market, not elsewhere
Because the lag before a recession can stretch beyond a year
Because the curve automatically returns to a normal slope within a few weeks
quiz.explanation: This indicator has held true across most US recessions, but the gap between an inversion and an actual recession has ranged from a few months to over two years. Being right about the direction but wrong about the timing can still be very costly.

quiz.question: What does a duration of 7 mean when rates rise by 1%?
options: You must hold at least 7 years to break even
The bond has 7 years left until maturity
The bond's yield rises to 7%
The bond's price falls by roughly 7%
quiz.explanation: Duration measures price sensitivity to interest rates, not maturity. It's also why betting on the direction of rates using long-maturity bonds amplifies both gains and losses.

keyTakeaways: Reading a yield curve: comparing short- and long-term yields to identify a trend
An inverted curve: a strong economic warning signal, not one to dismiss
Higher duration amplifies both gains and losses when rates move

practicePrompt.question: You notice a 2-year government bond yielding more than a 10-year one - unusual relative to the norm. How do you 'read' an economic signal from this, and what is that analytical step called?
options: This is just a random coincidence between two maturities, carrying no economic meaning
Short yields sitting above long ones is an inverted curve, which usually signals recession expectations
This phenomenon always means inflation is about to spike in the short run, unrelated to recession
There's no way to draw economic meaning from a yield gap between different maturities
practicePrompt.explanation: Reading a yield curve: comparing short- and long-term yields to identify a trend. An inverted yield curve (short maturity yielding more than long) has historically signaled recession with high accuracy (~80%) - one of the most closely watched economic indicators by investors and central banks alike.

application.title: Read today's yield curve
application.message: Look up the 2-year and 10-year US government bond yields right now, compare which one is higher, and draw your own conclusion about what the market expects for the economy ahead.
application.secondary: This exercise takes only a few minutes but gives you a genuine macro perspective.

sections.text: Understanding yield curve theory is one thing - applying it to read a real economic cycle is another. The simplest method professional investors use every day: compare the 2-year government bond yield against the 10-year yield.

When the 2-year yield exceeds the 10-year yield, that's a clear inversion signal - the market believes today's rate level is unusually high and will have to come down to respond to slowing growth or a recession. During 2022-2023, the US yield curve inverted the deepest in over 40 years as the Fed hiked rates aggressively to fight inflation - many economists used this signal to forecast a recession, though the exact timing always remained hard to pin down.
An investment strategy when expecting rates to fall

If a bond investor believes rates are about to drop sharply (say, because they expect the central bank to pivot toward easing), the sensible strategy is to buy long-maturity bonds instead of short ones. The reason lies in duration: long-maturity bonds have higher duration, so when rates fall, their prices rise far more than short-maturity bonds - producing a larger capital gain if the call is right. Conversely, if you expect rates to rise, leaning toward short-maturity bonds minimizes price losses.
When the curve flattens: a more ambiguous signal

A yield curve doesn't always give a clear upward-sloping or inverted signal. When the curve is nearly completely flat - yields across maturities nearly equal - that's usually a transition stage: the market isn't yet sure which way rates and the economy will move next, and may be near the peak of a tightening cycle before it turns. This is when you need to bring in other data (inflation, unemployment, GDP growth) rather than relying on the curve's shape alone.

items: Comparing the 2-year and 10-year yields: the fastest and most common way to read a yield curve's state
Expecting rates to fall → lean toward long-maturity bonds to maximize capital gain
Expecting rates to rise → lean toward short-maturity bonds to minimize price loss
A flat curve: an ambiguous signal that needs to be combined with other economic data
